name: Cunningham v. Gates
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California)
topic: Qualified immunity on interlocutory appeal after police shootings by a special surveillance unit; the duty to intercede requires a realistic opportunity; no constitutional right to be arrested before committing a crime; the vehicle jamming tactic; supervisory, council member, and city attorney liability
summary: Members of a Los Angeles Police Department surveillance unit watched two armed men rob a store, boxed in their getaway car with police vehicles, and a shootout followed in which one robber died and the other was permanently disabled; in a separate operation, officers shot a man they mistook for a fleeing armed robber. The Ninth Circuit held that officers who were not present, or who were present but had no realistic opportunity to intervene, cannot be liable for failing to intercede in a fellow officer's use of force. It also held there is no constitutional right to be arrested before one commits a crime, that the jamming tactic did not violate clearly established law on this record, and that council members and city attorneys were immune for indemnification decisions. It left the shooting officers and most supervisors to face trial.
coverage: The opinion, as amended, was read in full, including all 24 footnotes, from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/229/229.F3d.1271.98-56081.98-56077.98-55855.98-55108.98-55208.html. The archive marks headnote material as copyrighted material omitted; the court's opinion text is complete.

The citation 229 F.3d 1271, the docket numbers, the argument date of February 9, 2000, the filing date of September 15, 2000, the amendment date of October 31, 2000, and the panel (Hawkins and Thomas, Circuit Judges, and Magill, Senior Circuit Judge of the Eighth Circuit, sitting by designation; Magill writing) were confirmed from that file. The archive text does not print reporter page breaks, so references are to the opinion's numbered paragraphs as the archive presents them.

The district court opinions (989 F. Supp. 1256 and 989 F. Supp. 1262) and the state criminal record were not read. The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them, including the plaintiffs' allegations, which the court was required to credit at this stage.

The opinion refers to the plaintiffs' allegation that officers used jamming in an effort to provoke the use of force, and in footnote 23 declines to endorse any tactic that needlessly or unreasonably creates a dangerous situation. It does not apply or discuss the Ninth Circuit's later-named provocation rule. The Supreme Court's rejection of that rule in County of Los Angeles v. Mendez (2017), which has its own brief in this library, is noted for context only; Mendez was not re-read for this brief.
Subsequent proceedings in these cases, including any later Ninth Circuit decisions under the same name, were not researched.
facts:
The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them on interlocutory appeal from denials of summary judgment, with the plaintiffs' allegations taken as true where disputed (paras. 3-8, 54).

The Cunningham and Soly shootout. The LAPD's Special Investigation Section (SIS), a unit formed to interdict and apprehend armed, violent career criminals, received information in May 1995 connecting Robert Cunningham and Daniel Soly to an armed robbery. On June 26, 1995, SIS officers placed the two under surveillance and followed them to a liquor store in Newbury Park. The officers permitted them to rob the store although they had probable cause and the ability to arrest beforehand. After the robbers entered their getaway car, SIS officers used their cars to "jam" the vehicle into a confined space. According to the plaintiffs, the officers then opened fire without announcing themselves, with about eighteen shotgun blasts and handgun shots, killing Soly and permanently disabling Cunningham. The officers said Cunningham and Soly fired first, a version supported at Cunningham's criminal trial, where a California jury convicted him of attempting to murder the officers and of murdering Soly by provoking the officers to fire, and rejected his claim of self-defense (para. 3 and n. 14).

The Grover Smith shooting. On February 25, 1997, SIS detectives watched robbery suspect Michael Smith and three others rob a bar and flee by car. A helicopter tracked the car into a cul-de-sac; SIS units converged, muzzle flashes came from the suspects' car, and an armed man ran toward nearby houses. Detectives Winston and Spelman heard that the suspect was heading their way and saw a young man looking up and down the street and hiding briefly behind a tree. He was Grover Smith, a resident with outstanding warrants who assumed the helicopter was for him, yelled "They're coming for us," hopped a wall, and ran when he saw the officers' vehicle. Someone yelled "Freeze," and he was shot in the leg. The officers said he reached toward his waistband; Smith denied any threatening movement (paras. 4-8).

The lawsuits. The plaintiffs sued the City, the shooting officers, SIS officers who took part in surveillance but did not shoot, supervisors, police commissioners, council members, the mayor, and assistant city attorneys. They alleged a continuing course of unlawful conduct: surveil suspects, allow the robbery, jam the car, shoot whether or not a threat exists, and cover it up with false reports and testimony, all condoned by officials who ignored a code of silence and indemnified officers against punitive damages (paras. 10-18). The district court denied nearly all motions for summary judgment without analyzing each defendant's own conduct, relying in part on impeachment evidence known only to the court (paras. 23-27, n. 18).
holding:
Affirmed in part and reversed in part. Judge Magill wrote for a unanimous panel.

Scope of review. The court had jurisdiction only over purely legal qualified immunity questions, not over the Heck v. Humphrey ruling, the City's Monell appeal, or any denial of immunity resting on disputed material facts (paras. 32-44). Qualified immunity must be analyzed defendant by defendant, examining "the specific factual allegations against each individual defendant"; the district court's group analysis "fell far short" of that (para. 50).

Shooting officers. Because the district court found disputed facts about whether the officers had probable cause to use deadly force against Cunningham and Soly, the court lacked jurisdiction over their immunity and had to assume a constitutional injury could be proven (para. 54). For Smith, the dispute over whether he reached toward his waistband meant the shooting officers were not entitled to immunity at this stage (para. 55).

No right to be arrested. Quoting Hoffa v. United States, the court held that "[t]here is no constitutional right to be arrested" and that officers need not halt an investigation the moment they have probable cause. Allowing the robbery to occur stated no constitutional violation (paras. 60-61).

Failure to intercede. The defendants conceded that "police officers have a duty to intercede when their fellow officers violate the constitutional rights of a suspect or other citizen." But "officers can be held liable for failing to intercede only if they had an opportunity to intercede." Officers not present at the shootings could not intercede, and the undisputed evidence showed that the non-shooting officers who were present had no "realistic opportunity" to intercede. None could be liable on that theory (para. 62).

Jamming. Novel tactics can violate clearly established law if the force is unreasonable, and an officer who implements a policy in a patently unconstitutional manner is not immune. But the undisputed evidence showed jamming was neither new nor unique, had been used hundreds of times without incident, and was not used against these plaintiffs differently from past practice; and given armed suspects in the midst of a dangerous felony, it was a reasonable use of force. It was therefore not clearly established that jamming was unreasonable (paras. 64-70). The court said it was not endorsing any tactic "that needlessly or unreasonably creates a dangerous situation necessitating an escalation in the use of force" and was not holding jamming per se reasonable (nn. 23-24). As to Smith, jamming was too attenuated from his shooting, which followed the suspect's flight, an extended search, and Smith's own decision to run (para. 71).

Perjury and fabrication. Witnesses are absolutely immune for testimony; the plaintiffs offered "not an iota of evidence" of fabrication (paras. 72-73).

Supervisors and commissioners. Supervisors may be liable for culpable action or inaction in training, supervision, or control, for acquiescence, or for reckless or callous indifference. Because the district court found factual disputes, the court lacked jurisdiction to review their immunity, though it observed that evidence of supervisor misconduct seemed virtually nonexistent. It reversed as to Captain Koenig, who did not supervise the SIS until a month after the shootout (paras. 74-77).

Council members and city attorneys. Under Trevino v. Gates, discretionary, case by case indemnification of punitive damages in good faith compliance with California Government Code section 825(b) does not violate section 1983; the law was not clearly established before Trevino, and undisputed evidence showed good faith review after it. Both groups were immune (paras. 78-89). The plaintiffs lacked standing for injunctive relief (para. 90).
notDecided:
Whether the shootings were excessive. The court assumed, without deciding, that the plaintiffs might prove a constitutional injury from the shootings, and left the shooting officers to trial (paras. 54-55). It made no finding that any officer used excessive force.

Whether the supervisors and commissioners acquiesced in a code of silence. The court lacked jurisdiction over those fact bound denials, while signaling skepticism about the evidence (para. 76).

Whether Heck barred Cunningham's and Soly's claims. The court lacked jurisdiction but, in footnote 21, expressed serious disagreement with the district court and encouraged the parties and the new judge to revisit the issue.

Whether jamming is reasonable as a general matter. The court said it was not holding jamming per se reasonable; its ruling rested on the plaintiffs' failure to rebut evidence of long, incident free use (n. 24).

Any provocation theory. The plaintiffs alleged that jamming was used to provoke force, and the court said it did not endorse tactics that needlessly create danger (n. 23), but the opinion did not apply any rule under which a tactical choice makes a later reasonable shooting unlawful. The Supreme Court rejected the Ninth Circuit's later provocation rule in County of Los Angeles v. Mendez (2017), which has its own brief in this library.

Municipal liability. The City's appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (para. 43).
inPractice:
The holding Dr. Sowards teaches from Cunningham is the shape of the duty to intercede. The City conceded the duty exists: officers must step in when a fellow officer violates someone's constitutional rights. The court then drew the limit. Liability requires an opportunity to intercede, and for officers present at a sudden shootout the question is whether there was a realistic opportunity. Officers who were not at the scene, and officers who were there but could not have stopped gunfire that erupted in seconds, cannot be liable on that theory.

That limit cuts both ways. In a gunfight there is usually no realistic opportunity and no liability. In a prolonged use of force, a prone restraint that continues after control, a beating, repeated Taser cycles on a cuffed subject, or a jail extraction that goes on after the prisoner stops resisting, the opportunity is real and so is the exposure. Rodriguez v. County of Los Angeles, in this library, shows supervisors held liable for watching and not stopping exactly that kind of force. The test is the same.

Two other points matter for field officers. There is no constitutional right to be arrested; officers need not move the instant they have probable cause. And a tactic used many times without incident, used the same way again against armed felony suspects, is unlikely to be treated as clearly unconstitutional, but the court was careful not to bless any tactic that needlessly creates a dangerous situation. Tactical choices still get reviewed for reasonableness.

Finally, liability is individual. Each officer's exposure rests on what that officer did or could have done, not on membership in a unit.
trainIt:
Teach Cunningham in the supervision and intercede line as the case that defines the element of opportunity. Build the lesson around a spectrum of scenarios and ask, for each officer present, whether a realistic opportunity to intervene existed: a sudden exchange of gunfire lasting seconds (none); a partner's strikes continuing after a subject is cuffed (yes); a restraint where the subject has stopped moving and weight remains on the back (yes); a cell extraction where strikes continue on an unconscious prisoner (yes). The duty is real, the test is opportunity, and most force encounters that end in litigation last long enough for the opportunity to exist.

Train intervention as a skill, not a slogan. Give officers the words and the physical actions to stop a fellow officer's force, and practice them, so that when the opportunity exists the officer can act.

Train supervisors on the Larez formulation the court quoted: liability for culpable action or inaction in training, supervision, or control; for acquiescence; or for reckless or callous indifference. The reversal as to the captain who had not yet taken command shows that supervisory liability tracks actual authority at the time.

For tactics instructors, teach footnotes 23 and 24 with the holding. Long, documented, incident free use of a tactic supported immunity here, but the court did not endorse tactics that needlessly create a dangerous situation and did not hold the tactic per se reasonable. Document tactical training and its history.

Teach the posture. Cunningham was an interlocutory appeal. The shooting officers and most supervisors were sent back for trial. The court found no excessive force; it decided who was immune as a matter of law.

The facts include allegations the court was required to credit on summary judgment; the officers' version was supported by Cunningham's criminal conviction. The district court opinions and later proceedings were not read. The reference to County of Los Angeles v. Mendez is contextual; Cunningham itself did not apply a provocation rule.

applications.title: The duty to intercede is conceded; the test is opportunity
applications.body: Officers have a duty to intercede when a fellow officer violates someone's rights, but can be liable only if they had a realistic opportunity to do so. Officers not present, or present at a sudden shootout, had none. Officers present for a prolonged use of force usually do.

applications.title: There is no right to be arrested early
applications.body: Quoting Hoffa, the court held that officers need not halt an investigation the moment they have probable cause. Letting the robbery occur before moving in stated no constitutional claim.

applications.title: A proven tactic is not a blessed tactic
applications.body: Jamming had been used hundreds of times without incident and was used the same way here against armed felony suspects, so it was not clearly unconstitutional. The court said it was not endorsing any tactic that needlessly creates a dangerous situation and was not holding jamming per se reasonable.

applications.title: Liability is individual
applications.body: The court required an analysis of each defendant's own conduct and rejected group liability built on a department wide theory. It reversed as to a captain who did not take command until a month after the shootout.

applications.title: Teach the posture
applications.body: The shooting officers and most supervisors were sent back for trial. The court made no finding that anyone used excessive force; it decided who was immune as a matter of law.

quiz.q: Under Cunningham v. Gates, when can an officer be held liable for failing to intercede in a fellow officer's use of excessive force?
options: Whenever the officer is a member of the same unit
Only if the officer had a realistic opportunity to intercede
Whenever the officer was on duty anywhere in the city at the time
Never; there is no duty to intercede
quiz.teach: The defendants conceded the duty to intercede exists. The court held that liability requires an opportunity to intercede, and that officers who were absent or present at a sudden shootout with no realistic opportunity cannot be liable.

quiz.q: What did the court hold about the officers' decision to let the robbery occur even though they had probable cause to arrest beforehand?
options: It was deliberate indifference supporting municipal liability
There is no constitutional right to be arrested, so it stated no constitutional violation
It made the later shooting per se unreasonable
quiz.teach: Quoting Hoffa v. United States, the court said officers are under no constitutional duty to halt an investigation the moment they have the minimum evidence for probable cause.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit decide about whether the SIS officers who shot Cunningham, Soly, and Smith used excessive force?
options: It held the shootings were reasonable because the suspects were armed robbers
It held the shootings were excessive as a matter of law
It did not decide; disputed facts meant it lacked jurisdiction as to Cunningham and Soly, and the shooting officers in Smith's case were not immune at this stage
It held the officers were absolutely immune
quiz.teach: On interlocutory appeal the court could decide only legal questions. It assumed the plaintiffs might prove a constitutional injury and left the shooting officers and most supervisors to trial.
